811.quote_or_event: “Friendship with the self-willed Manmukhs lasts for only a few short days. This friendship is broken in an instant; this friendship leads to corruption.”
811.explanation: Guru Amar Das warns that friendship with the manmukh, the person ruled by his own ego, is short-lived and drags one toward vice however warm it seems.
811.tie_back: The Kural says that even when people of poor character seem fond enough to drink you in, it is better for that friendship to shrink than grow; Guru Amar Das explains why, since such friendship is brittle and corrupting.
811.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 587, Raag Vadhans (Vadhans ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
811._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on the worthlessness of friendship with people of bad character, though it lacks the Kural's image of excessive show of affection and its advice to let the bond dwindle gradually.

812.quote_or_event: “The true society is the company of those who meditate on the Name of the Lord. Do not associate with those, O Nanak! Who look out only for their own interests.”
812.explanation: Guru Arjan contrasts true company, built around the Name, with association with people who are only after their own advantage, and tells the Sikh to avoid the latter.
812.tie_back: The Kural describes unworthy people who befriend you when there is gain and leave when it ends; Guru Arjan names the same self-interested companions and says not to keep their company at all.
812.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 520, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
812._accuracy_note: A close match on self-interested companions; the Kural's shrug that such friendship is neither gain nor loss is replaced here by a firm instruction to avoid it.

813.quote_or_event: “Farid, when there is greed, what love can there be? When there is greed, love is false. How long can one remain in a thatched hut which leaks when it rains?”
813.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that love mixed with greed (lab) is false and gives no lasting shelter, like a leaking hut in the rain.
813.tie_back: The Kural puts the friend who weighs what he stands to gain in the same class as the hired companion and the thief; Farid likewise says love that calculates its profit is not love at all.
813.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1378, Salok Sheikh Farid 18 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
813._accuracy_note: Close on calculating, gain-driven affection being false; Farid's salok is primarily about love for God, and it does not make the Kural's comparison with paid companions and thieves.

814.quote_or_event: Before the battle of Bhangani (1686 or 1688), a body of Pathans who had taken service with Guru Gobind Singh on the recommendation of Pir Buddhu Shah were bought over by the hill raja Bhim Chand with promises of plunder, and most of the Udasis also deserted. Hearing of this, Pir Buddhu Shah came with his sons and several hundred followers to fight at the Guru's side, and two of his sons were killed.
814.explanation: The episode sets companions who abandoned the Guru on the eve of battle against an ally who arrived when it mattered and paid for it with his sons' lives.
814.tie_back: The Kural says it is better to be alone than to have companions like an untrained horse that throws its rider in mid-battle; the hired Pathans at Bhangani were exactly such companions, while Pir Buddhu Shah showed what a true ally is.
814.source: Wikipedia, 'Battle of Bhangani', citing Harjinder Singh Dilgeer and the Bachittar Natak (paraphrase)
814._accuracy_note: A vivid historical match for allies who fail in battle; Wikipedia is used as a last resort and sources differ on the year and some names, though the desertion of the Pathans and Pir Buddhu Shah's support are widely reported.

815.quote_or_event: “In this world, I have seen love to be false. Whether spouses or friends, all are concerned only with their own happiness. All say, “Mine! mine!”, and attach their consciousness to you with love. But at the very last moment, none shall go along with you. How strange are the ways of the world!”
815.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur observes that those who profess love and call us their own are moved by their own comfort, and none of them stands by us when it finally counts.
815.tie_back: The Kural says the paltry friendship of small-minded people, who give no protection even when you have done everything for them, is better never gained; Guru Tegh Bahadur describes those who claim us lovingly yet are not there at the decisive moment.
815.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 536, Raag Devgandhari, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
815._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit on companions who fail us when protection is needed, but the Guru's point is the final hour of death rather than worldly danger, and he does not draw the Kural's conclusion that such friendship is better not gained.

816.quote_or_event: “Friendship with a fool never works out right. As he knows, he acts; behold, and see that it is so.”
816.explanation: Guru Angad says that however close one becomes to a fool, the fool still acts only according to his own limited understanding, so the friendship can never come right.
816.tie_back: The Kural says being a stranger to the wise is worth ten million times more than the closest friendship with a fool; Guru Angad gives the reason, since intimacy cannot change how a fool acts.
816.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
816._accuracy_note: Matches the Kural's verdict on intimate friendship with a fool, but the other half of the comparison, the worth of mere acquaintance with the wise, is not in the salok.

817.quote_or_event: “If my heart is pure, and I am slandered, then the slanderer washes my clothes. One who slanders me is my friend”
817.explanation: Kabir says the person who attacks him with slander actually does him good, washing away his faults, so he counts such a critic as a friend.
817.tie_back: The Kural says what comes to you from enemies is worth far more than the friendship of those who only laugh along with you; Kabir likewise finds real benefit in his detractors, which no flattering companion can give.
817.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 339, Raag Gauree, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
817._accuracy_note: Shares the paradox that an adversary can do more good than a friend, but Kabir speaks of slander as spiritual cleansing and does not mention the hollow, laughing friends the Kural condemns.

818.quote_or_event: “If a fool does a job, he cannot do it right. Even if he does something right, he does the next thing wrong.”
818.explanation: Guru Angad observes that a foolish person spoils whatever task he takes up, so his help cannot be relied on.
818.tie_back: The Kural speaks of those who ruin a task that could easily be done and advises letting their friendship slacken quietly; Guru Angad describes the same unreliable helper who spoils what he is given to do.
818.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
818._accuracy_note: Next-best match: it describes the person who spoils a task, but the Kural's target feigns inability rather than lacks it, and the Kural's tactful counsel to let the friendship fade unannounced has no parallel here.

819.quote_or_event: “Farid, there are dozens who say they are friends; I search, but I cannot find even one.”
819.explanation: Farid laments that many claim friendship in words, but when he looks for one who is a friend in deed, he cannot find any.
819.tie_back: The Kural says friendship with those whose deeds differ from their words is painful even in a dream; Farid names the same gap between people who call themselves friends and the friendship that is actually there.
819.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1382, Salok Sheikh Farid 87 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
819._accuracy_note: Captures the gap between friendship professed in words (galeen) and friendship in reality, though Farid's salok continues as a longing for the divine Beloved, and the Kural's image of pain even in a dream is absent.

820.quote_or_event: “Kabir! I have seen a person who is as shiny as washed wax. He seems very clever and very virtuous, but in reality, he is without understanding, and corrupt.”
820.explanation: Kabir describes a person whose polished outward show of virtue hides a corrupt nature within.
820.tie_back: The Kural warns against even slight contact with those who are friendly in private but revile you in public; Kabir's polished but corrupt man shows the same split between the face he presents and what he is.
820.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir 139 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
820._accuracy_note: Matches the double-faced character in general, but Kabir's contrast is outer show versus inner corruption rather than private friendliness versus public slander, and it gives no instruction to keep away.
